Elnathan
el-nā'than
n. (a prince of Judah under Jehoiakim, son of Achbor, who fetched the prophet Urijah out of Egypt to his death and afterward pleaded with the king not to burn the scroll of Jeremiah)
From Hebrew Elnathan, compounded of El, God, and nathan, he gave — God hath given. The same name is borne by three of Ezra's messengers to Casiphia and by the grandfather of Jehoiachin.

Biblical Definition

Elnathan the son of Achbor is one of the most instructive minor figures in the closing years of Judah, because Scripture shows him doing an evil thing and a right thing within ten chapters, and never resolves the man into a type. He first appears as the king's agent in an extradition: “And Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, namely, Elnathan the son of Achbor, and certain men with him into Egypt” (Jer 26:22). The errand was to recover the prophet Urijah, who had fled for preaching what Jeremiah preached, and its end is stated without softening: they “fetched forth Urijah out of Egypt, and brought him unto Jehoiakim the king; who slew him with the sword” (Jer 26:23). Elnathan carried a faithful prophet home to be murdered. Yet when Jehoiakim sat in his winterhouse cutting Jeremiah's roll with a penknife and casting it in the fire, Elnathan is one of three men who spoke: “Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them” (Jer 36:25). He sat among the princes in the scribe's chamber when the roll was read (Jer 36:12), and something in the reading moved him. He is very probably the Elnathan of Jerusalem whose daughter Nehushta was the mother of Jehoiachin (2Ki 24:8), which makes him grandfather to a king. Scripture leaves him there: a man who did the state's dirty work and then risked the state's displeasure, and whose end is not recorded.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Elnathan; in sacred history he is a prince of Jehoiakim's court, son of Achbor, sent into Egypt after the prophet Urijah.

ELNATHAN, n. God hath given; a proper name of several men in the Hebrew Scriptures.

Chiefly, a prince in the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, the son of Achbor.

He was sent into Egypt to bring back the prophet Urijah, who was there slain by the king.

He was among the princes who heard the roll of Jeremiah read in the scribe's chamber.

Three men of the name were sent by Ezra to Casiphia to obtain ministers for the house of God.

Key Scripture

Jer 26:22 — "And Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, namely, Elnathan the son of Achbor, and certain men with him into Egypt."

Jer 36:12 — "Then he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Achbor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes."

Jer 36:25 — "Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them."

Ezr 8:16 — "Then sent I for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, and for Elnathan, and for Jarib, and for Elnathan, and for Nathan, and for Zechariah, and for Meshullam, chief men; also for Joiarib, and for Elnathan, men of understanding."

Modern Corruption

The modern instinct is to grade Elnathan on balance — a decent man in a bad job. Scripture neither excuses the extradition nor cancels the intercession, and thereby refuses the accounting altogether.

expand to see more

The therapeutic reading of Elnathan is that he was conflicted, that he did what he had to do, and that his later protest shows his heart was in the right place. Scripture will not have it. Urijah is dead, and Elnathan fetched him. The intercession over the roll does not undo that; it is simply the next thing he did, and it was right. Both facts stand in the record with no verdict attached, and the effect is to strip away the arithmetic by which men reckon themselves acceptable — the ledger of good outweighing bad which is the natural religion of every fallen heart and the flat contradiction of justification by faith alone.

What the passage does teach plainly is the impotence of private conscience inside public complicity. Three princes pleaded, “but he would not hear them” (Jer 36:25), and the roll burned anyway. A man in office who has already lent his hands to one injustice has spent the moral weight he would need for the next. The Reformed doctrine of the lesser magistrate is precisely the answer Elnathan did not give: an officer under an unrighteous command is not a neutral instrument, and the time to refuse is the first errand, not the second.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Elnathan (H494), God hath given; El (H410), God; nathan (H5414), to give; sar (H8269), prince, official; megillah (H4039), roll, scroll.

expand to see more

Hebrew Elnathan (H494) — God hath given; the name of the prince and of Ezra's messengers.

Hebrew El (H410) — God; the theophoric element opening the name.

Hebrew nathan (H5414) — to give, bestow; the verb closing it.

Hebrew sar (H8269) — prince, chief, official; his rank in the scribe's chamber.

Hebrew megillah (H4039) — roll, scroll; the burnt book he pleaded for.

Usage

"“Elnathan the son of Achbor, and certain men with him into Egypt” — the errand that killed a prophet."

"“Had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll” — the protest that came too late to matter."

"“For Elnathan… men of understanding” — the name borne later by better men in Ezra's train."
